articles.title: Calgary stays under water-use limit for fifth straight day; about three and a half weeks of restrictions may remain
articles.dek: Crews are finishing draining the old Bearspaw South feeder main and will start round-the-clock work to connect the new pipe, despite a valve problem over the weekend.
body: Calgary's daily water use has stayed below the 500-million-litre limit for five days in a row, City officials said in an update on Monday, Nov. 9 [1]. The limit is the level the City says it must stay under to keep the water system out of what it calls the red zone while the Bearspaw South feeder main is out of service [2].

City-wide Stage 4 restrictions began on Nov. 4 so crews could connect the new Bearspaw South feeder main to the water system [2]. While the existing main is shut down, the City is relying mainly on the Glenmore Water Treatment Plant, and the restrictions apply to every resident and business [2]. Neighbours in Airdrie, Chestermere, Strathmore and Tsuut'ina Nation are also asked to cut back [2].

Michael Thompson, chief operating officer of the City's water utility, said on Monday that draining of the old main was expected to finish that day, and crews have been excavating at two of the three locations where the new pipe will be joined [1].

What is new since last week is a setback at the third location, the Parkdale site, where a valve problem had to be repaired over the weekend [1]. Thompson said excavation along Parkdale Boulevard did not progress as much as crews wanted, but he said he did not believe the problem would delay the overall schedule [1].

Crews will begin working 24 hours a day, seven days a week at the 89 Street N.W. site to connect the feeder main, work Thompson said should take about two weeks [1]. He said there is no precise end date yet, but if everything goes well about three and a half weeks of restrictions remain [1]. Once the work is done, the original main will be turned back on so restrictions can end, and the new pipe is expected to be operating in mid-December after it is filled, flushed and tested for water quality [1][2].

Separately, a leak was found on a different feeder main at Edgemont Drive near Edgemont Boulevard N.W., which is not connected to the Bearspaw project [1]. Thompson said a repair plan is in place and that main will be taken out of service at some point this week, leaving the system with less backup capacity, though he said no widespread impacts are expected [1].
Mayor Jeromy Farkas thanked residents for cutting their use and asked them to keep it up until the project is finished [1]. "We know that we can do this," Farkas said [1].

Under the restrictions, residents are asked not to use water outdoors, including for flooding backyard skating rinks, to run dishwashers and washing machines only with full loads, to flush only when needed and to keep showers to about three minutes [2]. The City posts daily water-use figures against the 500-million-litre target [2].

Valve problem at the Parkdale site fixed over the weekend; no overall delay expected
Round-the-clock connection work at 89 Street N.W. expected to take about two weeks
About three and a half weeks of restrictions may remain; new pipe expected in service mid-December

articles.title: Calgary's living wage rises 40 cents to $26.90, the smallest increase in five years
articles.dek: Vibrant Communities Calgary says lower rents for smaller units pulled the figure down for single people and single parents, while transportation costs climbed more than 10 per cent.
body: The hourly wage a worker in Calgary needs to cover basic living costs is $26.90 in 2026, up 40 cents from $26.50 last year, according to figures released on Monday, Nov. 9, by Vibrant Communities Calgary with the Alberta Living Wage Network [1]. It is the smallest year-over-year rise in five years; between 2024 and 2025 the figure went up by just over $2 [1].

A living wage is an estimate of what a household must earn to pay for necessities in a given community. Alberta's minimum wage is $15 an hour, has not changed since 2018 and is the lowest in Canada, which puts Calgary's living wage nearly 80 per cent higher [1].

Transportation was the fastest-rising cost for every household type the group measured, climbing by more than 10 per cent [1]. At the same time, the calculated living wage fell for single-person and single-parent households, mostly because one- and two-bedroom units cost less [1]. The organization credited the City of Calgary's Home is Here housing strategy along with provincial and federal spending on affordable housing [1].
Calgary's figure is close to Toronto's living wage of $27.60 and well above Edmonton's $22.65 [1]. The gap between Calgary and Edmonton has grown from $1.45 in 2023 to $4.25 this year [1].
Twenty Alberta municipalities released living wages on Monday [1]. Banff had the highest at $27.45 an hour and Medicine Hat the lowest at $18.05 [1].

Michelle James, who speaks for the organization's living wage initiative, said many Calgarians depend on minimum-wage jobs to support their families [1]. The release also featured the heads of a housing association and a family and mental health nonprofit that pay a living wage, and Mayor Jeromy Farkas commented on the figures in relation to the provincial minimum wage [1].

articles.title: Grey Cup arrives in Calgary as soldiers hurt in CFB Wainwright fire are honoured
articles.dek: The trophy was carried into the Mewata Armoury with bagpipes and a military escort, opening a week of celebrations before Sunday's game at McMahon Stadium.
body: The Grey Cup arrived in Calgary on Monday, Nov. 9, with bagpipes and a Canadian Forces escort, at a ceremony that also honoured soldiers caught in a deadly fire at an Alberta military base last month [1][2].

The trophy was brought to the Mewata Armoury in a horse-drawn wagon before being marched inside [2]. Col. Kyle Clapperton, commander of 41 Canadian Brigade Group, told the gathering that the Cup's arrival marks both a celebration and a time for reflection. "This year that reflection carries special significance," he said [2].

Four soldiers died on Oct. 17 during a training exercise at CFB Wainwright, southeast of Edmonton, and dozens of others were injured when strong, sudden winds pushed flames from a nearby grass fire toward a group of 84 soldiers from Princess Patricia's Canadian Light Infantry [2]. Clapperton said many of the injured are reservists from 41 Brigade who serve with the Loyal Edmonton Regiment and the Calgary Highlanders [2].
CFL commissioner Stewart Johnston said the league is thinking of the Armed Forces community and described the Cup's arrival as the start of a week of celebrations [2].
The Edmonton Elks will face the Montreal Alouettes for the trophy at McMahon Stadium on Sunday, Nov. 15 [2].

articles.title: October referendum projected to cost $84 million, Elections Alberta says
articles.dek: A legislature committee approved a $59.6-million supplemental budget covering referendum operations and early work on the 2027 provincial election.
body: Elections Alberta projects that the province-wide referendum held on Oct. 19 will cost $84,268,919, the agency said in a release dated Nov. 6 [1].

Chief Electoral Officer Gordon McClure asked for a supplemental budget of $59,552,176 for the 2026-27 fiscal year, and the legislature's Standing Committee on Legislative Offices approved it [1]. The request is made up of $49,558,434 for referendum operations, $9,000,000 to prepare for the 2027 provincial general election and $993,742 for added organizational capacity [1].

Voters could cast up to 10 ballots, one for each question, and ballots were counted by hand at hundreds of locations [1]. Elections Alberta said more than 22 million ballots were counted, which it says is more than all ballots cast in Canada in the 2025 federal election [1]. More than 47,000 Albertans worked on the vote, and the agency noted that its cost figures do not include that human effort [1]. Official results were released on Oct. 29 [1].

The agency said it has the lowest per-person cost for election events in the country and the lowest ratio of staff to electors of any election body in Canada [1]. It also said there have been 58 electoral events across Canada since January 2025, 37 of them in Alberta [1].

Next steps include updating the voter register, a full review of the referendum and a written report, and returning equipment and supplies, while preparation continues for the 2027 general election [1]. McClure described the vote as "an event of unprecedented scale and scope" [1].

articles.title: SAIT hospitality students attend international convention summit in Panama through new partnership
articles.dek: A partnership with the Calgary TELUS Convention Centre makes SAIT the first North American school in an international convention-industry education network.
body: Students and staff from the Southern Alberta Institute of Technology are in Panama City for an international conference running from Nov. 8 to 11, a trip made possible by a new partnership between SAIT and the Calgary TELUS Convention Centre [1].

The conference is the annual summit of the International Congress and Convention Association, which has held the event for 65 years [1]. Through the partnership, SAIT has become the first post-secondary institution in North America to join the association's ICCAUni initiative, which launched in 2024 and includes 15 academic institutions in 13 countries [1].

Students from SAIT's School of Hospitality and Tourism will attend information sessions and meet mentors working in the meetings and conventions industry [1]. Two students were selected to make the trip based on essay submissions [1].

Shawn Cheng, a regional director with the association, said the program was "created to bridge the gap between the classroom and the industry" [1]. Kurby Court, president and CEO of the Calgary TELUS Convention Centre, and Mona James, an academic chair at SAIT, also spoke about the partnership [1].
The arrangement adds a study-abroad option for SAIT students tied to the meetings and conventions sector [1].

articles.title: Wind warning for Calgary as gusts reach 100 km/h; warm, dry week ahead
articles.dek: Environment Canada issued a new yellow wind warning for Calgary on Sunday afternoon, with damaging gusts expected to ease in the evening ahead of a week of highs well above normal.
body: Environment and Climate Change Canada issued a yellow wind warning for the City of Calgary at 3:40 p.m. on Sunday, Nov. 8, rated as having a moderate impact [1]. The warning said damaging winds with gusts of 90 to 100 km/h would begin to ease in the evening [1].

At 5 p.m. Sunday, the weather station at Calgary International Airport recorded 11.1 C under mainly sunny skies, with a west wind of 43 km/h gusting to 66 km/h and relative humidity of 25 per cent [1]. The overnight forecast called for southwest winds of 40 km/h gusting to 60 km/h, and to 80 km/h at times in the early evening, before winds turn west and drop to 20 km/h gusting to 40 km/h overnight [1]. The low was forecast at 3 C [1].
Environment Canada advised residents to secure loose objects and asked people to report weather damage using the hashtag #ABStorm or by calling 1-800-239-0484 [1].

The rest of the week is forecast to stay dry and unusually mild [1]. Monday is expected to be mainly sunny with a high of 10 C, followed by a sunny 12 C on Tuesday [1]. Highs are forecast to climb to 17 C on Wednesday, Nov. 11, and 19 C on Thursday, before easing to 12 C on Friday and Saturday [1]. Overnight lows through the week are forecast to stay at or above freezing, between 1 C and 6 C [1].

Those temperatures are far above the seasonal normals Environment Canada lists for Calgary at this time of year, a high of 4 C and a low of -8 C [1]. The mild spell arrives while the city remains under Stage 4 outdoor water restrictions, which ban all outdoor watering of lawns, gardens, trees and shrubs, with an exception for edible crops, while the Bearspaw South Feeder Main is connected [2]. The City says Stage 4 began Nov. 4 and the shutdown is expected to last about four weeks [2].
Forecasts can change, and Environment Canada updates its warnings and forecast through the day [1].

articles.title: City reports five fireworks incidents and three fines on first night of Diwali weekend
articles.dek: City, police and fire officials thanked residents for following Calgary's ban on personal fireworks as Diwali and Bandi Chhor Divas celebrations got underway.
body: The City of Calgary and its safety partners thanked residents, faith groups and cultural organizations on Sunday morning for helping keep Diwali and Bandi Chhor Divas celebrations safe, as festivities began across the city over the weekend [1].

According to the City, five fireworks incidents were reported on Saturday, Nov. 7, and three fines were issued [1]. The City did not say how much the fines were or where in the city the incidents took place [1].

Personal fireworks remain prohibited in Calgary [1]. The City said the ban applies to fireworks bought outside the city and to fireworks ordered online [1]. It encouraged community groups that want fireworks to use permitted, professionally operated displays, and pointed to a permitted professional show held on Nov. 5 at the Diwali in Huxley event [1].

The statement was issued on behalf of Calgary Fire Department Fire Marshal Glenn Baxter, Calgary Police Service Staff Sgt. Geoff Gawlinski and Damian Cole, the City's deputy chief of community safety [1]. Gawlinski said police had worked closely with community organizations and members ahead of the festival, adding, "we're grateful for their collaboration and partnership" [1]. The partners said they hope the level of compliance continues through the rest of the celebrations [1].

The City asks residents to call 911 for a fire or other emergency, and to call the police non-emergency line at 403-266-1234 to report fireworks that are happening now [1]. Fireworks that have already taken place can be reported through a 311 request under Disturbance and Public Behaviour Concerns [1].

Diwali and Bandi Chhor Divas fall on Sunday, Nov. 8, but some groups marked the occasion a day early [2]. On Saturday, Alberta Premier Danielle Smith and other government officials attended a celebration held at the Rio Banquet Hall in northeast Calgary [2].

articles.title: Cavalry FC rallies past FC Supra du Québec to reach CPL final, will host Atlético Ottawa on Nov. 21
articles.dek: A 2-0 win at Spruce Meadows overturned a first-leg loss and sends Calgary's Canadian Premier League club to the final at home.
body: Cavalry FC beat FC Supra du Québec 2-0 on Saturday, Nov. 7, in the second leg of their Canadian Premier League semifinal, earning a place in the league final [1][2]. Caniggia Elva and Ali Musse scored for Calgary [1].

Cavalry went into the match at ATCO Field at Spruce Meadows trailing after losing the first leg 2-1 in Québec [3]. Elva scored with a half-volley in the 25th minute, and Musse added a second goal around the hour mark, giving Cavalry a 3-2 win on aggregate [2]. Supra goalkeeper Joakim Milli saved a penalty from Musse during the match, having also stopped a penalty in the first leg [2]. Canadian Soccer Daily reported that a Cavalry player was sent off after a melee involving a ballboy [2].

Before the match, Culture Alberta reported that under the league's rules a Cavalry win by two or more goals would see the club host the final in Calgary [3]. Atlético Ottawa won the other semifinal, beating Forge FC 3-2 at home after extra time for a 5-4 aggregate win, with Nicolas Fleuriau Chateau scoring three goals [2].

The CPL final is scheduled for Saturday, Nov. 21, at 1 p.m. Calgary time at ATCO Field, according to Canadian Soccer Daily, which described the match as a rematch between the two clubs [2]. The outlet noted the weather as a possible factor for a late-November match outdoors [2].
The same weekend, the Calgary Flames were scheduled to play at the Saddledome against the Philadelphia Flyers on Sunday evening, after hosting the Anaheim Ducks on Friday [3].

articles.title: Physicians now triaging patients at six Alberta emergency rooms after months of delay, premier says
articles.dek: Premier Danielle Smith said the emergency-room triage teams announced in January were in place as of Saturday.
body: Physicians are now triaging patients at six emergency departments across Alberta, Premier Danielle Smith said on Saturday, Nov. 7, during her province-wide radio show [1][2]. Smith said the triage teams were in place as of Saturday [1].

The provincial government announced the plan in January [1]. It followed the death of a 44-year-old man who waited nearly eight hours at the Grey Nuns Community Hospital emergency room in Edmonton to have his chest pain assessed; he died on Dec. 22, 2025 [1]. The Alberta Medical Association has said he was one of several patients who died around that time while waiting for care [1].

The rollout was delayed while the province and the Alberta Medical Association worked out operational details and physicians' contracts, The Canadian Press reported [1]. "It took longer than we hoped," Smith said [1].
The reports read for this article do not say which six emergency departments have the new triage teams, or whether any of them are in Calgary [1][2]. Calgary Insight could not confirm that detail.
A public inquiry into the Edmonton man's death is scheduled to resume in December [1].

articles.title: Former mayor rejects blame as details emerge from Bearspaw feeder main inspection report
articles.dek: The provincial inspection of Calgary's water utility traces missed reforms back a decade, and Opposition leader Naheed Nenshi says the report clears him.
body: More details and the first political responses have emerged from the independent municipal inspection of the City of Calgary's Bearspaw South Feeder Main, the water line whose failures in June 2024 and December 2025 led to city-wide water restrictions [1][2].

The inspection was carried out by David Goldie, who was appointed under the Municipal Government Act in March 2026 [2]. Water Canada reports that the final report went to the province in October and that the Government of Alberta released it publicly this week; the Lethbridge Herald describes Goldie as having released the report this week [1][2]. The report contains 20 recommendations on how the utility is managed and overseen [1][2].

Much of the new attention is on a 2015–16 review of the water utility by the consulting firm Raftelis Financial. According to the report, then-mayor Naheed Nenshi and his chief of staff received an advance briefing on the draft-final version, while the full report and most of its recommendations never went to council [1][2]. Five of nine priority recommendations were left out, and those five were nearly identical to reforms later proposed by the 2024 independent review panel on the feeder main [1][2]. The Lethbridge Herald reports that Goldie described the handling of that review as irregular and a missed opportunity [1].

The report also says the utility's capital spending from 2006 to 2024 averaged about 35 per cent below approved budgets, and that spending from 2016 to 2020 was 46 per cent below the national average [1][2]. It puts water lost to leaks at 23 per cent in 2025 and notes that a 2022 corporate realignment spread core utility duties across several City departments [1]. The water, wastewater and stormwater network serves more than 1.8 million people and has an estimated replacement value of $89.6 billion, according to the report [1].

Among the recommendations reported by the Lethbridge Herald are moving the water utility into an arm's-length corporation controlled by the municipality, having council hire a consultant to compare that model with integration into ENMAX and report back by the fourth quarter of 2027, keeping a register of the most critical assets and their risks, and treating water loss as a core performance measure [1]. The report also asks the province to consider whether Alberta law gives enough oversight of critical municipal infrastructure [1].

Nenshi, who now leads the Official Opposition NDP, said, "This report exonerates me in the matter" [1]. He also called the release of the report a distraction and accused the government of pursuing a personal vendetta that has cost taxpayers tens of millions of dollars [1].

Municipal Affairs Minister Dan Williams has said he will give the report careful consideration, and that its release is not an immediate decision on any directives to the City [1][2]. Day-to-day operation of the utility stays with the City while the minister reviews it [1]. The report notes that the City has already set up a Water Utility Oversight Board and named an acting chief operating officer, and says their success will depend on clearer decisions, accountability and reporting [2]. Neither article reported a response from the current mayor or council [1][2].

articles.title: Chinook brings wind warning with gusts up to 100 km/h overnight
articles.dek: Environment Canada warned of strong gusts across Calgary and nearby communities from Friday afternoon, with winds expected to ease Saturday morning.
body: Environment and Climate Change Canada issued yellow-level wind warnings for parts of southern Alberta on Friday, with strong winds expected throughout the day [2]. For Calgary, the warning called for gusts of 90 to 100 km/h through Friday afternoon and evening, easing gradually on Saturday morning [1]. The warning also covered Cochrane, Okotoks, Foothills County and Mountain View County, and a separate warning was issued for the Edmonton region [1].

The winds came with a chinook. Calgary's high on Friday was forecast at about 11 C, with about 12 C expected on Saturday and a sunny 12 C on Sunday [1]. The strongest gusts were expected along the foothills and on the west side of the city [1].

Environment Canada's warning said driving could be difficult for high-profile vehicles such as trucks, vans and those pulling trailers, and that loose objects could be tossed by the wind [1]. Roofs, fences, tree branches and temporary structures could be damaged [1]. Crosswinds on open stretches of road west of the city were expected to be the worst, and drivers on Deerfoot Trail, Stoney Trail and the Trans-Canada Highway were advised to slow down [1].
With no rain in the forecast and dry grass, the risk of grass fires was raised west of the city, and residents were advised against outdoor burning this weekend [1].

Downed power lines can be reported to ENMAX's 24-hour trouble line at 403-514-6100, which also takes outage reports, and fallen trees or branches on City property can be reported to 311 [1]. No outage counts or damage reports were included in the coverage that could be reviewed [1].
Strong winds have caused damage in Calgary before: a spring storm in April toppled trees, branches and power lines across the city, as did a windstorm last January [1].

articles.title: Alberta's economy grew 3.3 per cent in 2025, outpacing the national rate, province says
articles.dek: New Statistics Canada figures show Alberta's real GDP grew faster than Canada's for a fourth straight year, according to the finance minister.
body: Alberta's real gross domestic product grew 3.3 per cent in 2025, compared with 1.9 per cent for Canada as a whole, according to a statement from Finance Minister and Treasury Board President Jason Nixon on Friday [1]. The statement responded to Statistics Canada's provincial and territorial economic accounts for 2025, released the same day [1].

The gap of 1.4 percentage points made Alberta's growth the largest of the Prairie provinces, the government said [1]. It also said Alberta's growth was 2.3 percentage points higher than Quebec's, 1.5 points higher than Ontario's and 0.9 points higher than British Columbia's [1].

According to the statement, Alberta's GDP per person was almost $76,000 in 2025, the highest in Canada, compared with a national average of just over $60,000 [1]. The province said that works out to about 20 per cent more output per person than the national average [1].

The government credited trade, record housing construction and infrastructure investment for the growth, and said Alberta's GDP has outpaced the national average for four consecutive years [1]. "Alberta is Canada's economic powerhouse," Nixon said [1]. The statement says the province expects Alberta to outperform the national economy again in 2026, and that the government plans to keep taxes competitive and advance major projects [1].
The statement does not break the figures down by city and does not mention Calgary specifically, and the figures cover the 2025 calendar year [1].

articles.title: Alberta's unemployment rate jumps to 7.3 per cent in October; Calgary's edges up to 6.6
articles.dek: New Labour Force Survey figures show Alberta lost 24,000 jobs last month, while Calgary's unemployment rate rose more modestly.
body: Alberta's unemployment rate climbed to 7.3 per cent in October, up from 6.4 per cent in September, according to Statistics Canada's monthly Labour Force Survey released on Friday, Nov. 6 [1].
The province lost 24,000 jobs in October after adding 23,000 in September [1]. Alberta's rate is now 0.6 percentage points above the national rate of 6.7 per cent [1].

In Calgary, the unemployment rate rose to 6.6 per cent from 6.3 per cent the month before, a smaller increase than in the province as a whole [1]. Calgary's employment rate, the share of working-age people who have a job, stood at 65.8 per cent, the highest among cities in its size group [1]. Across Canada, the average employment rate was 60.8 per cent [1].
Elsewhere in Alberta, the Wood Buffalo-Cold Lake region had the highest employment rate at 70.5 per cent, and Red Deer's was 66.1 per cent [1].

Charles St-Arnauld, chief economist at Servus Credit Union, said Alberta's economy is still performing better than the rest of the country, but cautioned that this is not a sign of a strengthening economy [1].

Busuyi Okeowo of Calgary Economic Development described the city's labour market as resilient while noting signs of softness in the near term [1]. He pointed to renewed investment in the energy sector and continued population growth as factors supporting the local economy [1].

articles.title: Calgary water use under 500 million litres for a second day as feeder main draining nears completion
articles.dek: The City says draining of the old Bearspaw South Feeder Main should finish this weekend, while road cutting begins on Parkdale Boulevard and 89 Street N.W.
body: Calgarians used 490 million litres of water on Thursday, Nov. 5, the second day in a row that city-wide use stayed in the green zone below 500 million litres a day, the City of Calgary said on Friday [1]. On Wednesday, Nov. 4, the first day of the shutdown, use was also 490 million litres, which the City said was 24 million litres lower than the day before [2].

What changed since Thursday: the City says draining of the existing Bearspaw South Feeder Main, which began on Nov. 5, is expected to be finished over the weekend [1][2]. On Friday, crews set up equipment storage and traffic detours at 83 Street N.W., 89 Street N.W. and Parkdale Boulevard, worked with hydrovac equipment near Broadview Park, and were to begin cutting the road surface on Parkdale Boulevard and 89 Street N.W. [1]. The City has said it is looking at ways to ease rush-hour traffic on Parkdale Boulevard during the work [2].

Stage 4 outdoor water restrictions remain in effect city-wide, which means no outdoor water use, including flooding backyard skating rinks [2][3]. Fines for breaking the rules start at $3,000 [3]. The City is also asking residents to run only full loads in dishwashers and washing machines, flush only when needed and keep showers to three minutes or less [1].

The existing main is expected to be out of service for about four weeks while the new pipe is connected, with commissioning of the new pipe planned for December [3]. During the shutdown the Glenmore Water Treatment Plant is supplying about 80 per cent of the water for the city and region, and the Bearspaw plant about 20 per cent; normally Bearspaw supplies about 60 per cent [3]. The City says the two plants can supply 500 million litres a day, and use above that level could leave too little water for firefighting, lower water pressure or lead to a boil-water advisory [3].
A non-drinking river water pick-up station is open at the Ogden boat launch, 3303 Bow River Pathway, from 7 a.m. to 7 p.m. daily [3].

articles.title: Two men charged after a man was robbed, beaten and then struck by a car in Saddle Ridge
articles.dek: Police say the victim was left with life-threatening injuries in a parking lot on Saddletowne Circle N.E. in October.
body: Calgary police have charged two men in connection with an October assault in the northeast community of Saddle Ridge that left a man with life-threatening injuries, the Calgary Police Service said on Friday, Nov. 6 [1][2].

Police say that at about 4:15 p.m. on Friday, Oct. 16, officers were called to a serious altercation involving three men in a parking lot at 218 Saddletowne Circle N.E. [1][2]. According to police, two men approached the victim to retrieve what the release describes as documented evidence from him [1]. Police allege the man was robbed and then assaulted several times, and was left lying in the parking lot [1].
An unrelated vehicle then struck the injured man [1][2]. Police say the driver of that vehicle did not see him [1]. The man suffered life-threatening injuries [1][2].

A 34-year-old man is charged with one count of robbery and is next scheduled to appear in court on Monday, Nov. 30 [1]. A 25-year-old man is charged with one count of aggravated assault and is next scheduled to appear in court on Tuesday, Nov. 17 [1]. The charges have not been tested in court.

Police are asking anyone with information about the incident to call the non-emergency line at 403-266-1234 [1]. Anonymous tips can be given to Crime Stoppers at 1-800-222-8477, online at calgarycrimestoppers.org, or through the P3 Tips app [1].

articles.title: Committee backs easing density rules for new hotels in the Beltline ahead of December hearing
articles.dek: A temporary pilot would leave part of a hotel's floor area out of density calculations near the BMO Centre, where Tourism Calgary says 3,000 more rooms are needed.
body: A City of Calgary committee has endorsed a proposal to exclude part of new hotel developments in the Beltline from the city's density rules, aiming to ease an expected shortage of hotel rooms near the Culture and Entertainment District [1][2]. The proposal went to the Infrastructure and Planning Committee on Nov. 4 for a recommendation to council, and a public hearing of council is expected on Dec. 8 [2].

The changes would amend the Beltline Area Redevelopment Plan and the Centre City sections of the Land Use Bylaw [2]. The first change is a temporary pilot: inside a defined hotel policy area, part of a hotel's floor area would not count toward its density limit, known as floor area ratio, when a development permit is reviewed [2]. The City says a cap on how much density can be excluded is still being evaluated [2].

The policy area runs along the CP Railway to 12 Avenue between 8 Street S.W. and 1 Street S.E., and between 1 Street and Macleod Trail S.E. west of 5 Street S.E., including part of Stampede Park [2]. A second change would let the City consider relaxing rules on building massing and separation case by case [2]. The City notes the changes would not guarantee approval of any development permit [2].

The City says hotel supply has become a key constraint on growth, citing Tourism Calgary's estimate that 3,000 more hotel rooms are needed near the BMO Centre [2]. Calgary had more than 10.5 million visitors in 2025, who spent $3.3 billion, and downtown hosted 159 conventions and events that generated $241 million in economic impact [2]. Hospitality officials say a shortage of rooms would slow tourism growth as the district is rebuilt, and several hotel projects have been announced near Victoria Park, with two under construction [1].
Public outreach on the proposal ran from July to Oct. 7 [2].

articles.title: City adds new snow-clearing equipment and will trial a multi-lane wing plow this winter
articles.dek: Glenmore Trail, Macleod Trail and Memorial Drive stay first in line under the council-approved Priority Snow Plan.
body: The City of Calgary says its crews and contractors are ready to work around the clock this winter, and it has added new high-capacity snow-clearing equipment for the season [1].

Among the additions is a wing plow that can clear several lanes in a single pass, which the City says it will trial this year [1]. Chris Hewitt, the City's manager of mobility maintenance, said crews and contractors will be available 24 hours a day, seven days a week through the winter [1].

Snow clearing follows the Priority Snow Plan approved by council [1]. Under the plan, the busiest routes, including Glenmore Trail, Macleod Trail and Memorial Drive, are cleared first, along with City-maintained sidewalks, priority pathways and pedestrian overpasses [1]. Major transit routes and residential routes come next [1].

The City encourages residents to check its road conditions map at maps.calgary.ca/roadconditions before travelling, and to find information about snow clearing at calgary.ca/snow [1]. Residents can also learn about their own responsibility for clearing sidewalks next to their homes at calgary.ca/shovel [1].
The announcement did not include the number of crews or the snow-clearing budget for the season [1].

articles.title: Fire badly damages garage behind vacant, boarded-up home in Montgomery
articles.dek: No one was hurt in the Thursday morning fire on Mackay Road N.W.; the cause is under investigation.
body: A fire on Thursday morning, Nov. 5, caused severe structural damage to a detached garage behind a vacant home in the northwest community of Montgomery, the Calgary Fire Department said [1].

Crews were called at about 10 a.m. to the 2300 block of Mackay Road N.W. for a structure fire in a garage at the back of a single-storey residential property [1]. The department says the home was vacant, with its windows and doors boarded up and its utilities disconnected beforehand [1].
People in neighbouring homes left on their own, and no injuries were reported [1]. Firefighters kept the fire contained to the garage [1].
The cause of the fire is under investigation, and a fire watch crew has been assigned to the property [1].
The department noted that it is part of the city's Coordinated Safety Response Team, which works with the Calgary Police Service, Alberta Health Services and other City services [1].

body: Mayor Jeromy Farkas launched the City of Calgary's 2026 Support Local holiday campaign on Friday, Nov. 6, during a visit to businesses in Bowness and Montgomery [1]. The campaign, now in its eighth year, encourages Calgarians to shop at independent local businesses during the holiday season [1].

The City works with 15 business improvement areas across Calgary [1]. The Mainstreet Bowness business improvement area represents more than 60 independent businesses, and the Montgomery business improvement area more than 115, according to their executive directors, Kellie Freeman and Jessica Lapuz [1]. Montgomery's Light Up Montgomery event is scheduled for Saturday, Nov. 14, from 5 to 8 p.m. in Montgomery Town Square [1].

The City also pointed to recent figures for downtown, saying international visitor spending there rose 15.6 per cent from a year earlier, with overseas visitor spending up 12.2 per cent [1]. A Chill Downtown this Winter campaign will run from Nov. 16 to March 31, 2027, and a Winter Parking Contest running from Nov. 4 to Dec. 22 is giving away seven weekly prizes of $150 in parking credit [1].

The City said its Farm Stand Program, which ran from May 1 to Oct. 14, had 29 stands run by seven farmers, and its webpage was viewed more than 26,000 times [1]. Erin Chrusch leads the City's business and local economy team, which runs the campaign [1].

articles.title: Province tables bills on campus neutrality, deepfakes and consumer protection
articles.dek: One bill would bar Alberta's post-secondary institutions from taking public positions on political and social issues; others target intimate deepfakes and defective vehicles.
body: The Alberta government has introduced legislation that would prevent post-secondary institutions from taking public positions on political, social and ideological issues [1]. The bill was tabled in the legislature on Tuesday, Nov. 3, and would stop institutions from taking stances that depart from an academic purpose; it could affect codes of conduct for staff and students [1]. Further details, including the bill number, were not available at publication.

Other bills introduced this fall session were outlined in a newspaper column by Chantelle de Jonge, the MLA for Chestermere-Strathmore and parliamentary secretary for affordability and utilities, which presents the government's own description of the measures [2]. According to the column, one proposed law would require public institutions, including municipalities and post-secondary schools, to put merit first in hiring and promotion rather than quotas [2].

Another proposal would strengthen protections against non-consensual intimate deepfakes, including computer-generated images, video and audio, with fines of up to $10,000, up to two years in jail, or both [2]. A consumer protection package would include right-to-repair measures for farmers, car owners and consumers, lemon laws for defective vehicles, steps against credit fraud, clearer ticket pricing and a board to resolve property disputes [2].

The column also says the province is putting $25.8 million into six independent school projects in Calgary, Edmonton and central Alberta, creating more than 3,500 student spaces, and that new rules will require the Canadian and Alberta flags to fly outside school buildings starting Jan. 4, 2027 [2]. The column did not give bill numbers, and its descriptions are the government's own account [2].

articles.title: Federal budget names Calgary projects as Ottawa projects a $62.3-billion deficit
articles.dek: Budget 2026, tabled Thursday, lists a Calgary community centre and a defence quantum hub, and puts major federal transfers to Alberta at $9.2 billion next year.
body: The federal government tabled Budget 2026 on Thursday, projecting a deficit of $62.3 billion for 2026-27. It forecasts revenue of $540.3 billion and expenses of $602.9 billion before actuarial changes, with federal debt at 39.9% of GDP [1]. Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne presented the budget, which carries the title "Masters of our destiny" [2].

Calgary appears by name in two places. The list of projects the budget proposes to support through the Build Communities Strong Fund includes the Silver Springs Community Centre building expansion in Calgary, alongside two Edmonton projects [3]. The budget describes the fund as $51 billion over 10 years starting in 2026-27, and $3 billion a year after that [3]. The defence chapter notes that the Quantum Defence Innovation Secure Hub, part of the BOREALIS defence innovation program, was launched in Calgary [4].

Elsewhere in Alberta, the defence chapter lists future fighter capabilities at CFB Cold Lake, a chemical and biological laboratory and blast assessment centre at CFB Suffield, a western operating base for the Royal Canadian Air Force's CC-330 Husky fleet, and maintenance work across Alberta bases. It also proposes $25 million over two years and $3 million for the military family resource centre at CFB Wainwright after a deadly training incident there [4].
Three Alberta projects appear on the budget's list of projects referred to the federal Major Projects Office: Alberta High-Speed Rail, the Pacific Link Pipeline and Pathways Plus [5].

Finance Canada's transfer tables put Alberta's Canada Health Transfer at $7.04 billion and its Canada Social Transfer at $2.20 billion in 2026-27, a total of $9.24 billion, or $1,792 per resident. That is up from $8.71 billion in 2025-26. Alberta receives no equalization payment [6].

Several national measures reach households in every province, including Calgary. The budget proposes a one-time 2027 supplement to the Canada Groceries and Essentials Benefit, which it costs at $4.1 billion, and notes that the federal fuel excise tax relief has been extended to the end of January 2027, with rates restored to half their usual level until the end of March [3].
The Calgary Data Desk's Federal Budget 2026 section lists every measure in the budget, with its cost by year, and what the budget names in each province.

articles.title: Committee backs a pause on large data centre applications; council to debate
articles.dek: City council's executive committee voted 10-3 for a notice of motion seeking a temporary moratorium on land-use applications for large-scale data centres.
body: Calgary's executive committee on Tuesday approved, by a 10-3 vote, a notice of motion that would temporarily freeze new land-use redesignation applications for large-scale data centres. The motion now goes to a full meeting of city council for debate [1]. Reports have not given a date for that debate [4].

The motion is sponsored by Mayor Jeromy Farkas and councillors Jennifer Wyness (Ward 2), Raj Dhaliwal (Ward 5), Andrew Yule and John Pantazopoulos (Ward 6) [1][2]. It asks city administration to report by March 2027 on changes to the land use bylaw, including a definition of data centres at different scales, and to return by the end of 2027 with a study of their risks and opportunities, including environmental impacts and the effect on regional and municipal water servicing [2][3].

Sponsors pointed to unanswered questions about water consumption, electricity use, stormwater and wastewater needs and noise, and to concerns that utility bills could rise [3]. Pantazopoulos described the pause as 12 months on new redesignations for data centres [3]. Farkas said the city should regulate artificial intelligence data centres so Calgary does not become a "Wild West" [1]. The motion separates small and medium data centres, which it says resemble other commercial and industrial users, from hyperscale artificial intelligence and cloud campuses [2].

Rocky View County, Saskatoon, Mississauga and Oakville have already adopted similar pauses [1][2]. Ward 8 Coun. Nathaniel Schmidt said he supports the motion and wants the province to take a more active role [1]. The provincial government's House Leader has said its fall legislative agenda includes protections for data centre development, though details have not been released [1].

One application already in the system, LOC2026-0156, would redesignate undeveloped land east of 52 Street N.E. and north of Redstone to allow large industrial buildings, power generation and a data centre. It remains under review and continues through the city's process [1][2][3].

articles.title: Stage 4 water restrictions in effect while crews connect the new Bearspaw feeder main
articles.dek: All outdoor water use is banned for about four weeks, and the City is asking residents to help keep daily use under 500 million litres.
body: Stage 4 water restrictions took effect across Calgary on Wednesday, Nov. 4. The Bearspaw South Feeder Main is shut down for about four weeks while crews connect the new replacement pipe to the existing system. During the work, the Glenmore treatment plant supplies roughly 80% of the water for the city and region [1].

Under Stage 4, outdoor water use is prohibited, including watering lawns, gardens and trees, washing driveways, sidewalks and cars on the street, construction water use, filling pools and hot tubs, and outdoor snow or ice making, which rules out flooding backyard rinks [1][2]. Exceptions include indoor car washes and hand-watering edible crops [1]. Fines start at $3,000 [1].

Indoors, the City is asking residents to run dishwashers and washing machines only with full loads, flush only when needed, keep showers to about three minutes and fix leaks [1]. The aim is to keep daily demand below 500 million litres. Above that level, the City says, the system risks not having enough water for firefighting, low pressure, a possible boil water advisory or a treatment failure [1].
The restrictions also apply in communities served by Calgary's system: Airdrie, Chestermere, Strathmore and the Tsuut'ina Nation [3].

Crews are draining the pipe, cutting the existing main and installing custom pieces to join the new pipe, followed by welding, backfilling and water quality testing [2]. Commissioning is expected to run until mid-December, and the City expects the new feeder main to be fully operating by the end of 2026 [2][3]. Mayor Jeromy Farkas called the 11-month project a significant milestone and asked Calgarians to cooperate one more time [2]. Questions go to 311 [1].

body: Emergency crews responded to a house fire and explosion at a rural property in Foothills County, southeast of Calgary near Okotoks, on Thursday morning. Reports began coming in shortly after 7 a.m., and photos and videos of the fire circulated online [1][2].

The property is near Heritage Heights School, which closed for the day as a precaution. Students who arrive by bus were taken to École Percy Pegler in Okotoks, where parents could pick them up [1][2]. The area around the property was evacuated [2]. A resident of nearby Heritage Pointe described the blast as feeling like a bomb going off [1].

The Foothills County fire department handled the call. The Calgary Fire Department sent a crew from its Seton station but stood it down because the property is outside city limits; a department spokesperson said the county's crews did not need Calgary's help [1][2].

No one was believed to have been hurt, though that had not been confirmed, and officials had not given a cause for the fire or the explosion [1]. CTV News described the story as developing, with updates through the morning [3].

articles.title: Provincial inspection of Bearspaw feeder main finds long-standing weaknesses at the City
articles.dek: An independent inspector's report released Thursday makes 20 recommendations on how Calgary governs, funds and manages risk on major water infrastructure.
body: The Government of Alberta on Thursday released an independent inspection report on the City of Calgary's handling of the Bearspaw South Feeder Main, the water pipe that failed on June 5, 2024 and again on Dec. 30, 2025 [1].

The report was written by David Goldie, an independent consultant and corporate director who chaired the Alberta Energy Regulator board from 2020 to 2024. He was appointed inspector in March under the Municipal Government Act and delivered his final report to the province in October [1].

According to the province, the report identifies long-standing, systemic weaknesses in the City's governance, management of infrastructure risk, accountability and delivery of capital projects. It makes 20 recommendations [1].

The inspection reaches back to events as early as 2004, including a 2015-16 financial review of the City's utilities by the firm Raftelis. The report finds that the then mayor, Naheed Nenshi, and his chief of staff were briefed in advance on a draft-final version of that review, but that the full report and most of its recommendations were never presented to council. Five of nine priority recommendations from that review never went to council, and the report says they are nearly identical to recommendations made by the 2024 independent review panel on the feeder main [1].

The report also points to spending patterns. From 2006 to 2024, the City's capital spending averaged about 35% below approved budgets, and from 2016 to 2020 capital spending by the water utility averaged 46% below the national average, according to the province's summary [1].

It says the City's governance did not consistently bring together information on infrastructure, finances and risk, and that risks flagged in earlier reviews were not consistently turned into inspections, funded work or corrective action [1].

The report acknowledges steps the City has taken, including starting a Water Utility Oversight Board and appointing an acting chief operating officer, and says their effectiveness is still to be judged [1].

Municipal Affairs Minister Dan Williams will review the findings and recommendations and decide whether to issue any directives. The province says releasing the report is not itself a decision on further action, and that day-to-day water operations remain the City's responsibility [1]. Williams said, "I will give the report the careful consideration it deserves" [1].
The report comes as Stage 4 water restrictions are in place across Calgary while crews connect the replacement feeder main. On Thursday the City said draining of the existing pipe was beginning [2].

articles.title: Committee backs $511-million bus lane option for Centre Street as Green Line north stalls
articles.dek: Executive committee endorsed studying curbside bus-only lanes for the Max Green route and $16.6 million in Green Line extension planning; council still has to decide.
body: City council's executive committee on Tuesday, Nov. 3, endorsed a push for faster improvements to the Max Green bus rapid transit route on Centre Street, after a city report put the cost of fully building it at no less than $511 million [1][2][3].

The report set out four scenarios. The lowest-cost one, about $511 million, would add curbside bus-only lanes from downtown to Keystone Hills, more Max stops, new terminals at 96 Avenue and 144 Avenue N., and a bus station in Crescent Heights. The most expensive, a fully separated transitway down the middle of Centre Street along the future Green Line alignment, is estimated at about $2.1 billion [1][3].

The report followed an amendment by Ward 3 Coun. Andrew Yule when council approved a revised downtown Green Line route in September [3]. Yule's motion, endorsed by committee, asks staff to report by mid-2027 on how curbside lanes would affect businesses, parking and loading, and on possible funding from other governments [2][3]. The Calgary Herald reported the committee vote as 9-2, with councillors Andre Chabot and Mike Jamieson opposed [3]. No money for the bus lanes has been approved, and the recommendation still needs a decision by full council [1][2].

Yule and Ward 4 Coun. DJ Kelly said the north leg of the Green Line LRT is unaffordable for now. Kelly cited high-level estimates of about $3 billion for a southeast extension to Seton and $4 billion for LRT north [1]. Yule said about 30,000 people use the Centre Street corridor each day [1][3]. "I need service now," Yule said [3].

Sarah Huber, the City's director of project development, said some bus lane work, such as land purchases and utility relocation, would still help an eventual Green Line [1]. Mayor Jeromy Farkas said he preferred an option that could later be converted to LRT [1].

Separately, administration said it will ask for $16.6 million in the coming four-year budget to plan the Green Line's extensions: $4.1 million for the southeast leg from Shepard to Seton and about $12.4 million to $12.5 million for the north leg from downtown to 160 Avenue N. Global News and the Herald give slightly different figures for the north leg [2][3]. Huber said this is planning and preliminary design, not construction [3]. Council will decide on that funding during budget deliberations later this month [2].
The first phase of the Green Line, from Shepard to 10 Avenue S. in the Beltline, is under construction with a budget of about $6.2 billion to $6.25 billion and is expected to open by 2031 [2][3].

articles.title: Fifth Safer Calgary operation leads to 10 people charged and 170 warrants executed
articles.dek: Police, peace officers, sheriffs and outreach workers ran a one-day operation on Wednesday in the downtown core, East Village and the Beltline.
body: The Calgary Police Service says the fifth Safer Calgary Operation Order, carried out on Wednesday, Nov. 4, led to 10 people being charged with a total of 18 charges and 170 arrest warrants being executed [1].

The operation brought together the police service, Calgary Community Safety, Transit Public Safety, Alberta Sheriffs, Emergency Health Services Alberta and community agencies. Teams enforced laws and bylaws, executed warrants, spoke with businesses and residents, and connected people with services [1].
Police reported attending 320 calls, issuing 99 summonses, making 330 proactive community engagements and making 165 referrals to social supports and outreach [1].

Among the highlights listed by police: two people were arrested in East Village for robbery and possession of illegal cigarettes. In the west end of downtown, officers seized 44 cartons holding more than 8,000 cigarettes, and the suspect was referred to Community Court under Alberta's Tobacco Tax Act. In the Beltline, two people were arrested and charged with assault after officers witnessed an assault in progress [1].

At the City Hall CTrain station, transit peace officers detained a person for a bylaw offence who matched an RCMP missing-person report and had outstanding warrants. Police also said a pregnant woman who needed housing was given a bed at the Navigation Centre reserved for police referrals [1].
The release does not name anyone charged or give court dates [1].

The operation follows earlier efforts called Safer Calgary – Operation CERTainty and the recently concluded Operation Restore [1]. Police Chief Katie McLellan said "simply accepting crime and social disorder is not an option" [1]. Public Safety and Emergency Services Minister Mike Ellis and Mayor Jeromy Farkas also commented in the release [1].

articles.title: Homicide unit lays murder charge in 2024 remand centre death and rules Skyview Ranch death a homicide
articles.dek: Police announced a second-degree murder charge in a death inside the Calgary Remand Centre, and said human remains found in Skyview Ranch were a homicide.
body: The Calgary Police Service Homicide Unit announced developments in two separate investigations this week [1][2].

On Tuesday, Nov. 3, police said they had charged a man in the death of another man who was in custody at the Calgary Remand Centre. Staff found the man unresponsive in his cell at about 11:20 a.m. on May 8, 2024. Life-saving efforts failed and he was declared dead [1].

After an autopsy by the Office of the Chief Medical Examiner, investigators deemed the death a homicide. Donny Paul Mills, 38, is charged with one count of second-degree murder. Police say he was also in custody at the time. He remains in custody and is next scheduled to appear in court on Monday, Jan. 4, 2027 [1]. The charge has not been tested in court.

Also on Tuesday, police said a death in northeast Calgary has been ruled a homicide. Officers were called to a home in the 200 block of Skyview Ranch Road N.E. for a welfare check on Oct. 27, and a search found evidence consistent with human remains [2].

An autopsy by the medical examiner's office is complete and the death has been deemed a homicide. Police say the person has been identified and that efforts to notify next of kin are continuing. The investigation is ongoing [2]. The police update itself does not name anyone charged in that case [2].
Police ask anyone with information on either case to call 403-266-1234 or contact Crime Stoppers anonymously at 1-800-222-8477 [1][2].

Accused next due in court Jan. 4, 2027

articles.title: Calgary home sales keep falling in October as condo prices slide further
articles.dek: The Calgary Real Estate Board's October figures show fewer sales, more supply in apartments and row homes, and a benchmark price of $564,200.
body: Calgary recorded 1,592 home sales in October, and sales so far this year are down nearly 11% from 2025, according to Calgary Real Estate Board (CREB) figures reported this week [1].

The Calgary Herald reported that October sales fell by more than 15% compared with October 2025, while new listings fell by more than 9% [2]. The two reports describe different measures: one compares the single month, the other the year to date [1][2].

Most of the decline came from apartment condominiums and row homes, though sales fell in every property type [1]. Inventory fell nearly 5% from a year earlier to 6,173 units, and months of supply sat just under four [1][2].

The overall benchmark price was $564,200, down less than 1% from October 2025 [1]. The apartment benchmark dropped 8% to $288,800, and REM reports it is now 15% below its August 2024 peak. Apartments have more than five months of supply [1][2]. The row home benchmark fell more than 5% to $407,500 with 4.4 months of supply [1][2].

Detached and semi-detached homes were close to balanced, with about three months of supply. The detached benchmark was $735,100 and the semi-detached benchmark $685,200, both little changed from a year earlier [1][2].

By district, prices rose in the City Centre and West, while the North East and East fell by about 6% [1][2]. CREB chief economist Ann-Marie Lurie said the downward pressure is mostly in "oversupplied higher-density segments" [2].

Nearby communities also saw lower benchmarks than a year ago. Cochrane's fell nearly 2% to $571,100 and Chestermere's more than 3% to $683,800, with both near six months of supply. Okotoks's benchmark eased to $600,100 [2].
key_facts: 1,592 sales in October; year-to-date sales down nearly 11%
Benchmark price $564,200, down less than 1% from a year ago
Apartment benchmark down 8% to $288,800
Inventory down nearly 5% to 6,173 units

articles.title: Council approves three new edge neighbourhoods; four more head to budget talks
articles.dek: The three approved communities are expected to hold about 3,965 homes, while four more would add 17,176 homes and need $377 million in capital in the coming budget.
body: Calgary city council has approved three new neighbourhoods on the city's edges, with four more applications to be considered during budget deliberations later in November, The Sprawl reported on Wednesday [1].

The three approved neighbourhoods are expected to hold about 3,965 homes combined. They do not need capital funding right away, but will need small operating amounts starting in 2028 and hundreds of millions of dollars in capital in future budget cycles [1].

On Oct. 27, council voted 9-6 to approve two Glacier Ridge applications on the city's northern edge. Mayor Jeromy Farkas and councillors Andrew Yule, John Pantazopoulos, Myke Atkinson, Nathaniel Schmidt and Harrison Clark voted against [1]. The Belvedere application on the eastern edge passed 11-4, with Farkas, Yule, Atkinson and Schmidt opposed [1].

Area councillor Jennifer Wyness pointed to a 22-kilometre feeder main under construction in north Calgary and a $24-million fire hall that was fast-tracked a year ago. Speaking about the risk of not following through on growth areas, she said, "You're going to strand assets if these fail" [1].

The four neighbourhoods still to come are expected to add 17,176 homes. City administration says they would need $377 million in capital in the upcoming four-year budget and nearly $1 billion more in later cycles [1].

The debate is tied to provincial Bill 28, which narrows what developers' off-site levies can pay for. Transit buses and fire trucks are now exempt, as are some fire hall costs beyond building code requirements. Administration confirmed that if developers do not cover those costs, property taxes make up the difference [1].

A committee directed administration to update council by Nov. 24 on Bill 28's estimated budget impacts. The City's proposed budget is to be released on Tuesday, Nov. 10, and the City plans to update its off-site levy bylaw in 2027 [1].
key_facts: Three approved neighbourhoods: about 3,965 homes
Four more proposed: 17,176 homes, $377 million in capital next budget
Glacier Ridge approved 9-6; Belvedere 11-4
Proposed City budget due Nov. 10

articles.title: Alberta gives local and Canadian firms priority on government purchases
articles.dek: A new provincial procurement policy, announced in response to tariffs, ranks qualified Alberta and Canadian businesses first for contracts under trade-agreement thresholds.
body: The Government of Alberta has announced a procurement policy that gives qualified Alberta and Canadian businesses a better chance at winning government contracts, citing the costs and uncertainty created by tariffs [1][2].

Under the policy, qualified Alberta businesses get priority consideration for purchases below the thresholds set by the New West Partnership Trade Agreement. Qualified Canadian businesses get priority for purchases at or above those thresholds but below the lowest applicable international trade agreement thresholds [1][2].

The measures apply to future purchases only, not to past contracts or work already under way. Existing vendor contracts will be reviewed before they are renewed or expire, to look for viable Alberta or Canadian alternatives [1][2]. The province says the rules will be applied within its legal and trade obligations [1].
The province buys about $7 billion a year in goods, services and construction. About 95% of that already goes to Canadian businesses, including 72% to businesses based in Alberta [1].

The release notes that the United States is Alberta's largest trading partner, with more than $152 billion in goods exported there in 2025. It says Alberta continues to oppose tariffs and retaliatory measures and will keep working with other provinces and Ottawa toward a return to trade without tariffs [1][2].

Premier Danielle Smith said the province is "putting local businesses first, supporting Canadian suppliers" [1]. The government also pointed businesses to a new page of tariff-related resources and encouraged private industry to follow a similar approach [1].
The provincial release is dated Nov. 4. A Black Press report said the announcement was made Nov. 3 [1][2].

articles.title: Mayor says proposed provincial electoral map shortchanges Calgary
articles.dek: A new advisory panel report would give Calgary 28 electoral divisions, but Mayor Jeromy Farkas and two dissenting panel members say the city should have more.
body: Calgary Mayor Jeromy Farkas says a proposed new map of Alberta's provincial electoral divisions does not give Calgary fair representation, LiveWire Calgary reported on Wednesday [1].

On Nov. 2 the province released a report from an independent advisory panel to the legislature's select special committee on electoral boundaries. It came about seven months after the Alberta Electoral Boundaries Commission's first report [1].

Both reports would raise the number of Calgary electoral divisions from 26 to 28. The new report increases the number of hybrid divisions, combining city and rural areas, from four to six. Bearspaw would be added to Calgary North West, and north and south Springbank to Calgary Bow and Calgary West [1].

Under the new map, Calgary divisions would average 56,726 people, or 5.6% above the provincial average, compared with 2.6% above it in the earlier report. Calgary-McKenzie, at 62,772 people or 17% above average, would be the most populous division in the province [1].

Farkas told reporters on Tuesday that Calgary is 84,101 people above the provincial average in net terms and urged residents to contact their MLAs [1]. "The current maps, as proposed, severely shortchange Calgarians," he said [1].

Two panel members, Gerard Kennedy and Brent Robinson, wrote a dissent that calls the map constitutionally fraught and predicts a court challenge. They also say changes to four northeast and east Calgary divisions seem unnecessary. Farkas and the dissenters both say Calgary should have about 1.5 more divisions [1]. Opposition NDP Leader Naheed Nenshi said Albertans should be concerned [1].

Elections Alberta has written to Speaker Ric McIver asking that the existing maps be used for the October 2027 election, or that the election be postponed. Justice Minister Mickey Amery said the government has no plans to change the date and hopes to approve new boundaries by the end of the fall sitting [1].

articles.title: Alberta drops parental income from student loan assessments for this school year
articles.dek: About 21,000 applications will be reassessed, and the change is expected to add about $118 million in provincial loans; student leaders welcome it but question the timing.
body: The Government of Alberta says it will stop counting parents' income when it decides how much provincial student loan money a student gets for the 2026-27 academic year [1][2].

Alberta Student Aid will reassess about 21,000 applications where parental income reduced a student's award. Students do not need to reapply or send documents; those who qualify for more funding will be notified and directed to their student aid portal [1][2]. New applications are being assessed without parental income starting in early November [1].

The province expects the change to add about $118 million in provincial loan disbursements this year, which it says fits within the $887-million budget for loan disbursements [1]. About 126,000 full-time applications were submitted between June 3 and Oct. 14, compared with about 125,000 over the same period in 2025 [1].

Only the parental income rule changes; other eligibility rules stay the same [1]. LiveWire Calgary reports that spousal income is still a factor. Parental and spousal income were dropped from assessments in 2012 and brought back earlier this year [2].
Advanced Education Minister Myles McDougall said being accountable means listening to people and looking at how decisions affect them [1].

Noel Ormita, president of the Students' Association of Mount Royal University, welcomed the change but said it came nearly three months into the school year, after some students may have deferred studies or taken jobs [2]. He said the earlier policy "would have created more financial barriers for students" [2]. He also criticized the consultation process and the spring decision to double the minimum student contribution from $1,500 to $3,000 [2].
The University of Calgary Students' Union declined to comment, and the SAIT Students' Association did not respond to LiveWire by its deadline [2].

articles.title: Calgary water use stays in the green zone as crews start draining the old feeder main
articles.dek: The city used 490 million litres on Wednesday, the first full day of Stage 4 restrictions, as work moved to draining the existing Bearspaw South Feeder Main.
body: Calgarians used 490 million litres of water on Wednesday, Nov. 4, keeping use in the City's green zone of less than 500 million litres a day, the City said Thursday [1].
That was 24 million litres less than the day before, according to the City [1]. Stage 4 restrictions took effect Wednesday while crews connect the new Bearspaw South Feeder Main to the system [1].

The City says crews began draining the existing feeder main on Thursday after setting up drainage sites, shutting down pumps and closing valves. Pathway users are asked to follow detours and stay clear of work sites [1].

Crews are also preparing for repairs on Parkdale Boulevard and near Broadview Park, and the City says it is looking at ways to improve traffic flow and reduce rush-hour delays on Parkdale Boulevard during the work [1].

To stay in the green zone, the City is asking everyone to stop all outdoor water use, including flooding backyard skating rinks, to run dishwashers and washing machines only with full loads, to flush toilets only when needed and to keep showers to three minutes or less. The restrictions apply to all residents and businesses [1].

On the same day, the province released an independent inspection report on the City's management of the feeder main, which failed in June 2024 and again in December 2025 [2]. More information on the restrictions is posted at calgary.ca/savewater [1].

articles.title: City Sport Hub coach named captain of Canada's national cricket team
articles.dek: Hamza Tariq, who coaches young players through the City's Sport Hub program, was named Canada's cricket captain this fall.
body: A coach with the City of Calgary's Sport Hub program has been named captain of Canada's national cricket team, the City said Thursday [1].
Hamza Tariq was named captain this fall. He also coaches through the Future Cricket Stars Academy, one of the local sport organizations that works with Sport Hub [1].

Sport Hub connects children and teens with qualified coaches from local sport organizations. It brings programs into schools and communities, provides equipment, and offers community lessons at little or no cost [1].

The coaches in Sport Hub come from local sport organizations that partner with the City, and Tariq is one of them through Future Cricket Stars Academy [1]. The City's announcement presents his appointment as bringing international experience to Calgary children and teens [1].
Tariq coached cricket during the Sport Hub pilot at Crossing Park School in the northeast community of Martindale, according to the City [1].
Brett Whittingham, a recreation programs leader with the City, said the program wants "kids learning from people who know the sport" [1].
The City says families can find programs and registration information at calgary.ca/SportHub [1].
